beats.intro: Lesson twelve. [[sub]]The planning process: what will be demanded of you, where you stand, and how to close the gap.
beats.gas: Planning sounds lofty. It isn't. [[drive]]Driving to work, you glance at the gas gauge. [[need]]You estimate how far you have to go, and how much gas that takes. [[have]]You compare it with what is in the tank, [[decide]]and decide whether to stop. That is planning.
beats.steps: The breakfast factory planned the same way. [[f1]]First, forecast demand. [[f2]]Second, work out what the factory will produce if nothing changes. [[f3]]Third, reconcile the two by adjusting production starts. [[g]]Any plan follows these steps. [[g1]]What will your environment demand of you? [[g2]]Where will you be if you do nothing different, counting what is already in the pipeline? [[g3]]And what more, or less, must you do?
beats.env: Step one: your environment. Treat your group as if it were its own company. [[mail]]Take the mailroom. [[cust]]Its customers are the rest of the company. [[vend]]Its vendors supply postage meters and mail carts. [[comp]]It has no internal competitor, but an outside parcel service makes a good benchmark. [[look]]Look at what customers expect and how they see you, at new technology that could replace what you do, at your vendors, and at the other groups your work depends on.
beats.diff: Look at two time frames: [[now]]what your environment demands now, [[year]]and what it will demand a year from now. [[gap]]If today's work meets today's demand, then everything new you take on should answer the difference. Your response to that difference is the real outcome of planning.
beats.honest: At this step, don't think about what you can actually do. [[mkt]]Suppose marketing knows it can sell a hundred units a month, [[doubt]]but doubts the factory can make more than ten, [[ten]]so it forecasts ten. [[never]]Then the factory never tools up for the real demand. [[sep]]State demand honestly, and deal with capacity in step three.
beats.status: Step two: present status. [[list]]List your current capabilities and the projects in the works. [[curr]]Count them in the same currency as demand. If demand is finished designs, your pipeline is partly finished designs. [[when]]Note when each will come out. [[loss]]And expect losses. In semiconductor manufacturing, only about eighty percent of the material started is finished. [[mgr]]Allow for some loss in managerial projects too.
beats.gap: Step three: close the gap. [[need]]First ask what you need to do. [[can]]Then, separately, what you can do. [[will]]Then decide what you will do, and how much of the gap it will close, and when. [[strat]]That set of actions is your strategy.
beats.strat: Strategy or tactics? [[def]]Your strategy is the most general summary of what you plan to do. Your tactics are how you carry it out. [[comm]]A communications manager decides to link every plant by electronic mail. That is his strategy. [[room]]The mailroom manager's strategy is to put printers in the mailroom and deliver printouts around the building. [[same]]The mailroom manager's strategy is the communications manager's tactics.
beats.bruce: Grove's first example: a marketing manager. [[three]]He had three people, a huge inventory of projects, all of which had to be finished, and no budget to hire. [[narrow]]A full match was impossible, so he narrowed the gap. [[moves]]He moved non-critical tasks to less qualified but less busy groups, brought in a summer student for well-defined work, and monitored his group closely. [[long]]For the longer term, he shared work with similar groups and cut duplication. [[req]]And he asked to grow, with his plan as the case.
beats.cindy: Grove's second example: a process engineer bringing new chip processes into production. [[env]]Her environment: untested processes and tools, and the people who pull at her. Development wanted less testing and paperwork; production wanted more. [[cust]]Her customer was production; her vendors were the engineering groups. [[status]]Her present status: development's data always arrived incomplete, because it was low on their list. [[plan]]Her strategy: define every step a new process must pass, set dates by working back with time offsets, [[agree]]get development's manager to agree the schedule, [[mon]]then monitor her vendors weekly and publish how they did: an indicator, and a window into the black box.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Plan in three steps: demand, present status, close the gap. [[w2]]Look at demand now and a year out; respond to the difference. [[w3]]State demand honestly, before thinking about capacity. [[w4]]Count your pipeline in the same currency, and expect losses. [[w5]]Your actions to close the gap are your strategy. Now the lesson practice.
